patterns.title: Rescue loans that paid the foreign lenders
patterns.summary:
In one crisis after another from 1995 to 2018, emergency loans from the IMF, the US Treasury, European governments and the European Central Bank arrived while foreign banks and bondholders were pulling money out. The official money kept debts paid on time, so private lenders could leave whole or nearly whole, and the debt moved onto the public books of the borrowing country and its official lenders. Mexico 1995: a $48.8 billion package (up to $20 billion from the US Exchange Stabilization Fund, $17.8 billion from the IMF, $10 billion via the BIS) let Mexico pay off its dollar-linked tesobono bonds, which fell from $29.2 billion to $0.7 billion during 1995 (GAO 1996); foreign mutual funds and other investors held $17 billion of $28 billion outstanding (PIIE). East Asia 1997–98: under IMF programmes, foreign bank claims on Korea fell by $38.9 billion, on Thailand by $28.6 billion and on Indonesia by $13.9 billion between mid-1997 and end-1998 (de Brouwer, RBA 1999); Japanese banks held over 30% of claims on Asia and European banks 47% (BIS 1998). In Korea, creditor banks were persuaded by their home governments on 24 December 1997 to roll over loans, which were then swapped into Korean sovereign debt (IMF IEO 2003).

Greece 2010: the IMF's own 2013 evaluation says debt restructuring was ruled out by the euro area, partly because of risks to euro-area banks, and that the delay let private creditors reduce their exposure while debt moved into official hands, leaving the official sector "on the hook". BIS data show French and German banks held $958 billion of claims on Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain at end-2009. Ireland 2010: ECB President Trichet's letter of 19 November 2010 told Ireland to seek a rescue or lose ECB emergency support to its banks; the €67.5 billion EU-IMF package followed, and the Oireachtas inquiry found the ECB's position helped place bank debts on Irish citizens. UK banks had $230 billion and German banks $177 billion of exposure to Ireland. Argentina received IMF increases to $22 billion in 2001 and a record $57 billion in 2018; the IMF's 2021 evaluation says residents' capital flight and redemptions drained the 2018 money and the programme failed its aims. Counter-cases: in Russia 1998 the IMF paid $4.8 billion and Russia still defaulted on 17 August, with foreign GKO holders shut out; in Latvia 2008 the Nordic parent banks agreed to keep their money in.

countries.note: 1995: $48.8bn multilateral package (US up to $20bn, IMF $17.8bn, BIS $10bn, Canada $1bn). Tesobono debt fell from $29.2bn to $0.7bn in 1995; Mexico repaid the US ESF in full in January 1997 (GAO 1996; PIIE).

IMF SBA of about $21bn approved 4 Dec 1997; foreign banks agreed a rollover on 24 Dec 1997 and swapped short-term loans for 1–3 year sovereign debt (IMF IEO 2003). Foreign bank claims fell $38.9bn, mid-1997 to end-1998 (de Brouwer 1999).
Foreign bank claims fell from $69.4bn to $40.8bn (−41%) between June 1997 and December 1998, during the 1997–98 crisis (de Brouwer, RBA 1999). Package size not documented here.
IMF SBA of about $10bn approved 5 Nov 1997, with $8bn assumed from the World Bank and ADB (IMF IEO 2003). Foreign bank claims fell from $58.7bn to $44.8bn, mid-1997 to end-1998 (de Brouwer 1999).

December 1998: IMF about $18bn plus about $15bn of bilateral loans via the BIS and Japan; international bank rollover rates averaged only 65–70%, and Brazil lost about $14bn of reserves in two days before floating the real (IMF IEO 2003).

$22.6bn package approved July 1998; IMF paid a first tranche of $4.8bn on 20 July. Russia defaulted and devalued on 17 August 1998; foreign GKO holders were excluded from later central bank deals (Hedlund, Demokratizatsiya).

IMF arrangement raised to $13.7bn (Jan 2001), then $22bn (Sept 2001); the IMF's evaluators say support should have stopped earlier (IEO 2004). 2018: record $57bn SBA; IMF's 2021 evaluation cites capital flight and says the aims were not met.

2010 programme: IMF's 2013 ex post evaluation says the euro area ruled out restructuring and that the delay let private creditors cut exposure, shifting debt to official lenders (IMF CR 13/156, paras 31, 55–57).

ECB letter of 19 Nov 2010 pressed Ireland to seek a rescue; €67.5bn EU-IMF package followed (AP via Fox News 2014). The Oireachtas Banking Inquiry (2016) found the ECB's stance helped place bank debts on citizens.
€7.5bn IMF-EU-Nordic package agreed December 2008 (IMF PR 09/304). The four Nordic parent banks of its largest foreign-owned banks pledged in Sept 2009 to keep their exposure (IMF).

BIS: French banks had $493bn of claims on Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain at end-2009. French chair told the IMF board in May 2010 its banks would support Greece (reported leaked minutes, The Press Project).

BIS: German banks had $465bn of claims on Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain at end-2009, including $177bn on Ireland; public-sector exposure to Spain, Greece and Portugal equalled 12.1% of their Tier 1 capital. German banks held 13% of claims on Asia at end-1997 (BIS).
BIS: UK banks had $230bn of exposure to Ireland at end-2009, the largest of any country's banks; 8% of reporting banks' claims on Asia at end-1997 (BIS 1998).
The Dutch chair, with the French and German chairs, conveyed its banks' commitments to the IMF board in May 2010, according to leaked minutes reported by The Press Project (2014).

Japanese banks held over 30% of claims on Asia and withdrew $38bn in the six quarters to December 1998, over 40% of loan repayments from the region (de Brouwer, RBA 1999). Japan also lent bilaterally to Brazil in 1998 (IEO 2003).

Swedbank and SEB, parents of two of Latvia's four largest foreign-owned banks, signed the Sept 2009 Stockholm pledge to keep exposure (IMF). Sweden's finance minister backed the Latvian programme in Dec 2008 (openDemocracy).
DnB NORD A/S, parent of DnB NORD Banka in Latvia, signed the Sept 2009 pledge to maintain exposure (IMF).
Nordea Bank Finland, parent of Nordea's Latvian branch, signed the Sept 2009 pledge to maintain exposure (IMF).

US Treasury lent Mexico through the Exchange Stabilization Fund without congressional approval; peak draw $11.5bn in July 1995, repaid January 1997 with a $580m profit to the Treasury (PIIE). The IMF is headquartered in Washington.

timeline.event: On 26 April the US, Canada and Mexico set up a $6bn plus C$1bn swap line, half of the US share from the Treasury's Exchange Stabilization Fund.
On 31 January President Clinton directs the Treasury to lend Mexico up to $20bn from the Exchange Stabilization Fund without congressional approval.
Mexico's dollar-linked tesobono debt falls from $29.2bn to $0.7bn by end-November as the rescue money arrives.
Mexico repays the US Exchange Stabilization Fund in full in January; the Treasury earns $580m over its own borrowing cost.
The IMF approves about $10bn for Indonesia on 5 November and about $21bn for Korea on 4 December.
On 24 December major international banks, urged by their home governments, agree to roll over Korea's short-term loans.
Japanese banks withdraw $38bn from East Asia in the six quarters to December 1998, over 40% of the region's loan repayments.
The IMF pays Russia a $4.8bn first tranche on 20 July; on 17 August Russia freezes short-term debt and lets the ruble fall.
Brazil gets about $18bn from the IMF and about $15bn from BIS-arranged and Japanese loans in December.
The IMF raises Argentina's arrangement to $13.7bn in January and to $22bn in September, setting $3bn aside for debt restructuring.
The IMF, EU and others agree a €7.5bn support package for Latvia in December.
On 11 September in Stockholm, four Nordic parent banks pledge to maintain their overall exposure to Latvia.
BIS data show French and German banks hold $958bn of claims on Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain at end-2009.
On 19 November ECB President Trichet writes to Ireland's finance minister that ECB emergency support depends on Ireland seeking a rescue.
The IMF's ex post evaluation of the 2010 Greece programme says delay let private creditors cut exposure and shift debt to official hands.
Trichet tells the Irish banking inquiry that the ECB did not blackmail Ireland and that burden-sharing was then widely seen as ill-advised.
The Oireachtas Banking Inquiry reports that the ECB position helped place large bank debts on Irish citizens.
ESMT Berlin researchers publish a draft study tracing where €215.9bn of Greek bailout money went.
The IMF approves a stand-by arrangement for Argentina, later raised to $57bn, the largest in its history.
The IMF's ex post evaluation says the 2018 Argentina programme did not restore confidence amid residents' capital flight.

claims_per_author.author: Jörg Rocholl and Axel Stahmer
claims_per_author.work: Where did the Greek bailout money go? ESMT White Paper WP-16-02 (2016, draft)
claims_per_author.claim: Rocholl and Stahmer say that of €215.9bn disbursed May 2010–June 2015, €9.7bn (under 5%) reached the Greek budget; €86.9bn repaid old debt, €52.3bn paid interest, €37.3bn recapitalised Greek banks and €29.7bn paid incentives to bondholders in the 2012 restructuring.
claims_per_author.status: Draft white paper, not peer-reviewed; the authors call the figures descriptive. Widely reported (e.g. GreekReporter, 5 May 2016, via Handelsblatt). The IMF's 2013 evaluation separately confirms that debt shifted from private to official holders.

claims_per_author.author: Dan Davies
claims_per_author.work: Greek banks were bigger beneficiaries of the 2010 bailout than French and German banks (Naked Capitalism repost, July 2015)
claims_per_author.claim: Davies says Greek banks held just under €40bn of Greek government debt in early 2010, against about €27bn for French and €25bn for German banks, so Greek banks gained most from the 2010 rescue.
claims_per_author.status: Based on Bruegel and BIS tables that Davies says may double-count; he agrees European financial stability was a major motive.

claims_per_author.author: The Press Project (reporting leaked IMF board minutes)
claims_per_author.work: IMF leak: European banks had committed to maintain exposure in Greek bonds (3 Feb 2014)
claims_per_author.claim: The Press Project says leaked minutes of the May 2010 IMF board show Brazil's director warning against bailing out Greece's private bondholders, mainly European financial institutions, and Dutch, French and German chairs promising their banks would stay in.
claims_per_author.status: Minutes not opened directly; the article says El País and the Wall Street Journal also reported them. It says those banks' Greek bond holdings fell from over $122bn to about $66bn by early 2012.

claims_per_author.author: Paul Gallagher (former Irish Attorney General)
claims_per_author.work: Evidence to the Oireachtas Banking Inquiry, reported by Irish Examiner, 18 July 2015
claims_per_author.claim: Gallagher says Irish taxpayers could have been spared more than €14bn paid to unsecured bondholders, and that troika approval was the only obstacle.
claims_per_author.status: The then government argued bondholders ranked equally with depositors; Trichet denied ECB threats (Irish Times 2015).

claims_per_author.author: Mats Engström
claims_per_author.work: Latvia's crisis: between Sweden and Europe, openDemocracy, 10 June 2009
claims_per_author.claim: Engström says, citing Affärsvärlden, that the IMF team first favoured devaluing the lats, the European Commission and Swedish government opposed it, and Swedish banks feared losses on Baltic loans if Latvia devalued.
claims_per_author.status: Swedish finance minister Anders Borg said Sweden only helped Latvia keep the currency regime it chose (same article). Not confirmed by the IMF records read.

claims_per_author.author: Senator Alfonse D'Amato
claims_per_author.work: As quoted in the PIIE study of the Exchange Stabilization Fund
claims_per_author.claim: D'Amato says the ESF was used to bail out global speculators in Mexico.
claims_per_author.status: The PIIE authors say the moral-hazard effect can be exaggerated and that many foreign investors in Mexico took large losses.

uncertain: The nationality of the foreign tesobono holders repaid in 1995 is not documented here; PIIE says only that foreign mutual funds and other investors held $17bn of $28bn.
Country-by-country foreign bank exposure to Korea, Thailand and Indonesia in 1997 was not found; only region-wide shares (Japan over 30%, Europe 47%, North America 10%) are shown.

Whether the 2010 Greek programme mainly protected French and German banks or Greek banks is disputed: the IMF 2013 evaluation and Dan Davies differ in emphasis, and the IMF board notice of June 2013 stresses that spillovers were contained.

The Buenos Aires Times reported the IMF's 2021 Argentina evaluation as describing a bailout to private creditors and carry-trade investors; the IMF's own press release does not use that wording, so how the evaluation frames it is not settled here.
The IMF's 2004 Argentina evaluation, in the parts read, does not directly say that IMF money financed private capital flight or debt service in 2001.
Trichet and the ECB deny that the ECB blackmailed Ireland or threatened to cut credit if Anglo Irish bondholders were burned.

patterns.title: Investors sue the state after privatization
patterns.summary:
Foreign companies that bought or ran privatized water, gas and power services used investment treaties to sue governments that froze tariffs, changed contracts or took services back. Most cases go to ICSID, the World Bank Group's arbitration centre in Washington. Two of the water deals were themselves tied to the World Bank: Bolivia's 1999 Cochabamba concession to Bechtel's Aguas del Tunari was part of a World Bank-backed privatization plan, and in Tanzania the World Bank and others lent $140m in 2003 on condition that a private firm run Dar es Salaam's water, which went to Biwater's City Water. Bolivia cancelled its contract after protests in April 2000; Tanzania ended Biwater's in May 2005 and deported its managers. Bechtel's claim was settled in 2006 with no payment for lost profits; Biwater won a finding of breach but $0 in damages (2008).

Argentina is the main target. After its 2001–2002 crisis measures, 46 treaty cases had been filed by March 2009 (Freshfields/Kluwer) and 50 between 2001 and 2012 (South Centre). Awards include CMS Gas $133.2m (2005), Azurix (an Enron water firm) $165.2m (2006), Enron $106.2m and Sempra $128.2m (2007, later annulled), BG Group $185.2m (2007), National Grid $54m (2008), Vivendi (Tucumán water) $105m (2007) and Suez/Vivendi/AGBAR/AWG $405m (2015, claim over $1bn). After the US suspended Argentina's trade preferences in 2012 over unpaid awards, Argentina settled five awards worth $677m in October 2013 with bonds of $506m face value, a 25% cut. Other tribunals rejected claims: Urbaser (Spain) got $0 in 2016, and Veolia's €174m claim over Alexandria's waste contract and Egypt's minimum wage rise was dismissed in 2018. Outside privatized services, Occidental was paid $980m by Ecuador (2016) and Vattenfall got €1.43bn from Germany (2021) over the nuclear phase-out.

countries.note: Aguas del Tunari (Bechtel subsidiary) won a 40-year Cochabamba water contract in 1999 under a World Bank-backed plan; Bolivia ended it in April 2000 after protests. ICSID ARB/02/3 under the Netherlands–Bolivia BIT was settled in January 2006 (bilaterals.org; italaw).

Biwater's City Water ran Dar es Salaam water from 2003 under a World Bank-financed project; Tanzania terminated it in May 2005. ICSID ARB/05/22: claim $20m, breach found, $0 damages (24 July 2008) (UNCTAD; IISD).

Respondent in 46 treaty cases by March 2009 (Freshfields/Kluwer) and 50 in 2001–2012, 27 of 36 fully public ones aimed at post-crisis measures (South Centre 2015). About $1.4bn in fixed compensation across 15 cases.

Veolia Propreté claimed €174m under the France–Egypt treaty over its 2000 Alexandria waste contract, partly over a minimum wage rise; the ICSID tribunal dismissed the claim in May 2018 (AFTINET via bilaterals.org).

Context, not a privatized service: Ecuador took Occidental's oil Block 15 in 2006; ICSID awarded $1.77bn in 2012, cut to about $1bn on annulment in 2015; Ecuador agreed to pay $980m (bilaterals.org, 2015–2016).

Context, not a privatization: Vattenfall claimed €4.7bn at ICSID under the Energy Charter Treaty over the nuclear phase-out; Germany settled in March 2021, paying Vattenfall €1.43bn (IISD; The Local).

US claimants against Argentina: CMS ($133.2m), Azurix ($165.2m awarded of $685m claimed), Enron ($106.2m), Sempra ($128.2m), LG&E ($57.4m), Continental Casualty ($2.8m). Bechtel owned Aguas del Tunari (Bolivia).
Vivendi (Compagnie Générale des Eaux) won $105m of $317m claimed over Tucumán water (UNCTAD); Vivendi was a claimant in the $405m Suez/AGBAR/AWG award (2015); Veolia sued Egypt.
Biwater Gauff (Tanzania): UK claimant (UNCTAD). BG Group plc won $185.2m (2007) and National Grid plc $54m (2008) against Argentina, both under UNCITRAL rules (Freshfields/Kluwer).
Urbaser and Consorcio de Aguas Bilbao Bizkaia sued Argentina under the Spain–Argentina BIT over Greater Buenos Aires water (AGBA); award of 8 Dec 2016 gave $0 damages (IISD).
Vattenfall, owned by the Swedish state, received €1.43bn from Germany in the March 2021 settlement (IISD; The Local).
Aguas del Tunari's claim against Bolivia was brought under the 1992 Bolivia–Netherlands bilateral investment treaty (italaw; bilaterals.org).

timeline.event: Vivendi and its Tucumán subsidiary Aguas del Aconquija file an ICSID claim against Argentina over its water concession.
Bolivia grants Bechtel's Aguas del Tunari a 40-year Cochabamba water contract under a World Bank-backed privatization plan; rates rise 100–200% for some.
After a general strike in January and protests in April, Bolivia terminates the Aguas del Tunari contract.
Azurix, an Enron subsidiary, files a claim against Argentina under the US–Argentina BIT after leaving its Buenos Aires province water concession.
Biwater's City Water signs contracts to run Dar es Salaam water, under a $140m World Bank-led project conditioned on private operation.
Tanzania terminates City Water's contract in May and deports its senior managers on 1 June.
First award against Argentina after the crisis: CMS Gas Transmission is awarded $133.2m on 12 May.
Bechtel's claim against Bolivia is settled in January; Bolivia states the termination was due to civil unrest, not company acts.
An ICSID tribunal awards Azurix about $165m against Argentina on 14 July; annulment is refused in September 2009.
Vivendi is awarded $105m over the Tucumán water concession in August.
On 24 July the Biwater tribunal finds Tanzania breached the UK treaty but awards no damages.
A Freshfields count lists 46 treaty cases against Argentina since 2001, with nothing yet paid.
The US suspends Argentina from its trade preference scheme over unpaid Azurix and Blue Ridge (CMS) awards.
An ICSID tribunal awards Occidental $1.77bn against Ecuador over the 2006 seizure of Block 15.
Argentina settles five awards worth $677m, paying bonds of $506m face value after a 25% cut.
On 9 April a tribunal orders Argentina to pay $405m to Suez, AGBAR, Vivendi and AWG over Buenos Aires water.
Ecuador agrees to pay Occidental $980m after an annulment committee cut the award.
On 8 December the Urbaser tribunal awards no damages and, for the first time, hears a human-right-to-water counterclaim, which it dismisses.
An ICSID tribunal dismisses Veolia's €174m claim against Egypt over the Alexandria waste contract.
Germany settles the nuclear phase-out claims; Vattenfall receives €1.43bn of the €4.7bn it sought.

Whether Argentina's 2001–2002 emergency measures were lawful is contested: tribunals rejected Argentina's necessity defence in CMS, Enron, Sempra and BG but accepted the treaty exception in LG&E and Continental (South Centre 2015).
Total sums actually paid by Argentina across all crisis cases are not established here; the 2013 settlement covered five awards, and the South Centre gives about $900m in final rulings by 2015.
Veolia's claim against Egypt was dismissed but the reasons were not published at the time, so how the minimum-wage issue was decided is unknown.
Who held the Azurix award by the time of payment, and the exact amount paid to each of the five 2013 claimants, are not given in the pages read.
